subproblems.title: Finite cyclotomic character with finite-field control and Frobenius values
subproblems.statement: Put Ω = AlgebraicClosure ℚ and G = Autℚ(Ω). For every positive natural number N, there exist a homomorphism χ : G → (ℤ/Nℤ)ˣ and an intermediate field F of Ω/ℚ finite-dimensional over ℚ such that: agreement of σ and τ on F implies χ(σ) = χ(τ); whenever ζ ∈ Ω satisfies ζ^N = 1, σ(ζ) = ζ^a for the least nonnegative representative a of χ(σ); and, for every prime ℓ not dividing N, every valuation subring P of Ω with ℓ a nonunit, and every arithmetic Frobenius σ at P above ℓ, χ(σ) equals the unit represented by ℓ modulo N.
subproblems.lean_statement: ∀ (N : ℕ) [NeZero N], ∃ (χ : (AlgebraicClosure ℚ ≃ₐ[ℚ] AlgebraicClosure ℚ) →* (ZMod N)ˣ) (F : IntermediateField ℚ (AlgebraicClosure ℚ)), FiniteDimensional ℚ F ∧ (∀ σ τ : (AlgebraicClosure ℚ ≃ₐ[ℚ] AlgebraicClosure ℚ), (∀ x ∈ F, σ x = τ x) → χ σ = χ τ) ∧ (∀ (σ : (AlgebraicClosure ℚ ≃ₐ[ℚ] AlgebraicClosure ℚ)) (ζ : AlgebraicClosure ℚ), ζ ^ N = 1 → σ ζ = ζ ^ ((χ σ : ZMod N).val)) ∧ (∀ (ℓ : ℕ) (hℓ : ℓ.Prime) (hℓN : ¬ ℓ ∣ N) (P : ValuationSubring (AlgebraicClosure ℚ)), P.LiesOverPrime ℓ → ∀ σ : (AlgebraicClosure ℚ ≃ₐ[ℚ] AlgebraicClosure ℚ), P.IsFrobeniusAt σ ℓ → χ σ = ZMod.unitOfCoprime ℓ ((Nat.Prime.coprime_iff_not_dvd hℓ).mpr hℓN))
subproblems.natural_proof:
1. Let μ_N = {ζ ∈ Ω : ζ^N = 1}. The polynomial X^N−1 splits in Ω and has no repeated roots, since its derivative N X^(N−1) is nonzero at every root in characteristic zero. Thus μ_N has exactly N elements. They are nonzero and form a multiplicative group.
2. Every finite multiplicative subgroup H of a field is cyclic. Let d be the least common multiple of its element orders. For each maximal prime power r^a dividing d, choose an element whose order has r-part r^a and raise it to the prime-to-r part of its order. This gives an element of order r^a. Products of these elements have order d: for commuting factors of coprime orders, a power of their product equal to one makes corresponding powers lie in the intersection of the cyclic subgroups; that intersection is trivial because element orders divide both coprime orders. Every element of H is a root of X^d−1. A nonzero degree-d polynomial over a field has at most d roots, by division by X−a and induction on degree. Therefore |H| ≤ d, whereas the constructed element has d distinct powers. It generates H. In particular, choose ζ₀ generating μ_N, of order N.
3. Each σ ∈ G acts bijectively on μ_N, so σ(ζ₀) = ζ₀^a for a unique residue class a modulo N. This power has order N exactly when a is coprime to N, since its order is N/gcd(a,N). Consequently a defines a unit χ(σ). Every root is a power of ζ₀, so σ(ζ) = ζ^a for every ζ ∈ μ_N. Taking the least nonnegative representative does not change these powers. Composition multiplies the exponents, and the identity has exponent one modulo N. Uniqueness of the exponent proves that χ is a monoid homomorphism.
4. Let F = ℚ(μ_N) inside Ω. This is finite-dimensional: adjoining one algebraic element gives a finite extension spanned by powers below its minimal-polynomial degree, and μ_N is finite. If σ and τ agree on F, they agree on ζ₀. Its order N then implies equality of the underlying residue classes and hence χ(σ) = χ(τ).
5. Fix a prime ℓ not dividing N and P with P.LiesOverPrime ℓ. Every ζ ∈ μ_N belongs to P. Otherwise the valuation property puts ζ⁻¹ in P, but ζ = (ζ⁻¹)^(N−1) then also belongs to P. Moreover ζ⁻¹ = ζ^(N−1) belongs to P, so ζ is a unit. The residue field k(P) has characteristic ℓ: the proper kernel of ℤ → k(P) contains (ℓ), because ℓ is a nonunit of P, and (ℓ) is maximal in ℤ.
6. Reduction is injective on μ_N. If ξ ∈ μ_N reduces to one and ξ ≠ 1, factor ξ^N−1 and cancel ξ−1 in Ω to obtain 1+ξ+⋯+ξ^(N−1) = 0. Reduction gives N = 0 in characteristic ℓ, contradicting ℓ ∤ N. Apply this to the quotient of two roots with equal reductions to prove injectivity.
7. If P.IsFrobeniusAt σ ℓ, σ preserves P and its induced action on k(P) is the ℓ-power map. Hence σ(ζ) and ζ^ℓ have equal reductions for every ζ ∈ μ_N. Both are in μ_N, so step 6 makes them equal. At ζ₀ this identifies χ(σ) with ℓ modulo N. Units are determined by their underlying values, so this is exactly the ZMod.unitOfCoprime in the statement.
8. For N = 1, μ_N = {1} and (ℤ/Nℤ)ˣ is trivial. The construction still works, and the least representative is zero, giving σ(1) = 1^0 = 1. Thus all assertions include this case.
proof_key_steps: Show that μ_N has N elements and is cyclic.
Define the character by the unique unit exponent and prove its homomorphism laws.
Use the finite field generated by μ_N to control the character.
Prove valuation-unit membership and injectivity of reduction away from N.
Identify arithmetic Frobenius with the specified residue-class unit.

subproblems.title: Unique unit-valued lift of compatible approximate characters
subproblems.statement: Let C be a commutative ring, G a group, and J an ideal such that C is complete and separated for its J-adic filtration. Suppose a_n : G → C satisfy a_m(g)−a_n(g) ∈ J^n for n ≤ m, a_n(1)−1 ∈ J^n, and a_n(gh)−a_n(g)a_n(h) ∈ J^n for all n,g,h. There is a unique homomorphism b : G → Cˣ such that b(g)−a_n(g) ∈ J^n for all n,g.
subproblems.lean_statement: ∀ {C G : Type} [CommRing C] [Group G] (J : Ideal C) [IsAdicComplete J C] (a : ℕ → G → C), (∀ (n m : ℕ), n ≤ m → ∀ g : G, a m g - a n g ∈ J ^ n) → (∀ n : ℕ, a n 1 - 1 ∈ J ^ n) → (∀ (n : ℕ) (g h : G), a n (g * h) - a n g * a n h ∈ J ^ n) → ∃! b : G →* Cˣ, ∀ (n : ℕ) (g : G), (b g : C) - a n g ∈ J ^ n
subproblems.natural_proof:
1. The ideal multiple J^n C equals J^n: ideal absorption gives one inclusion, and x = x·1 gives the other. Thus the compatibility hypothesis is exactly the ideal-adic Cauchy condition on n ↦ a_n(g), for each fixed g. Precompleteness supplies β(g) ∈ C satisfying β(g)−a_n(g) ∈ J^n for every n.
2. Such a scalar is unique. Two choices differ by an element of every J^n, so separatedness makes their difference zero. Choose these uniquely determined β(g) for all g.
3. For every n, β(1)−1 = [β(1)−a_n(1)]+[a_n(1)−1] belongs to J^n. Separatedness yields β(1) = 1.
4. For fixed g,h and every n, expand β(gh)−β(g)β(h) as [β(gh)−a_n(gh)] + [a_n(gh)−a_n(g)a_n(h)] + [a_n(g)−β(g)]a_n(h) + β(g)[a_n(h)−β(h)]. Every summand belongs to J^n, by the hypotheses and ideal absorption. Separatedness gives β(gh) = β(g)β(h).
5. Applying step 4 to g,g⁻¹ and to g⁻¹,g gives β(g)β(g⁻¹) = 1 and β(g⁻¹)β(g) = 1. Define b(g) as the unit with value β(g) and inverse β(g⁻¹). Equality of underlying values proves b(1) = 1 and b(gh) = b(g)b(h). This yields the required homomorphism, with the congruences from step 1.
6. If b′ is another such homomorphism, the underlying values of b′(g) and b(g) differ by an element of every J^n. Separatedness makes them equal. Extensionality of units and homomorphisms gives b′ = b, proving unique existence. Precision zero causes no exception because J^0 is the whole ring.
proof_key_steps: Apply precompleteness pointwise to the compatible sequences.
Use separatedness to obtain unique scalar limits.
Pass the identity and multiplication congruences to exact equalities.
Construct units using the value at the inverse group element.
Prove uniqueness by separatedness and extensionality.

subproblems.title: Adic cyclotomic character over a local coefficient algebra
subproblems.statement: Let 𝒪 be a characteristic-zero commutative discrete valuation domain, complete and separated for its maximal ideal 𝔫. Let p be prime with p ∈ 𝔫. Let R be a commutative local 𝒪-algebra whose structural map is local, and let 𝔪 be its maximal ideal. There exists a homomorphism c : Autℚ(AlgebraicClosure ℚ) → Rˣ such that, for each n ≥ 0, agreement on some intermediate field finite-dimensional over ℚ implies c(σ)−c(τ) ∈ 𝔪^n. Moreover, for every prime ℓ ≠ p, every valuation subring P lying over ℓ, and every arithmetic Frobenius σ at P above ℓ, the underlying value of c(σ) equals ℓ in R.
subproblems.lean_statement: ∀ {𝒪 : Type} [CommRing 𝒪] [IsDomain 𝒪] [IsDiscreteValuationRing 𝒪] [IsAdicComplete (IsLocalRing.maximalIdeal 𝒪) 𝒪] [CharZero 𝒪] (p : ℕ) [Fact p.Prime], (p : 𝒪) ∈ IsLocalRing.maximalIdeal 𝒪 → ∀ {R : Type} [CommRing R] [IsLocalRing R] [Algebra 𝒪 R], IsLocalHom (algebraMap 𝒪 R) → ∃ c : (AlgebraicClosure ℚ ≃ₐ[ℚ] AlgebraicClosure ℚ) →* Rˣ, (∀ n : ℕ, ∃ F : IntermediateField ℚ (AlgebraicClosure ℚ), FiniteDimensional ℚ F ∧ ∀ σ τ : (AlgebraicClosure ℚ ≃ₐ[ℚ] AlgebraicClosure ℚ), (∀ x ∈ F, σ x = τ x) → ((c σ : Rˣ) : R) - ((c τ : Rˣ) : R) ∈ IsLocalRing.maximalIdeal R ^ n) ∧ (∀ (ℓ : ℕ), ℓ.Prime → ℓ ≠ p → ∀ P : ValuationSubring (AlgebraicClosure ℚ), P.LiesOverPrime ℓ → ∀ σ : (AlgebraicClosure ℚ ≃ₐ[ℚ] AlgebraicClosure ℚ), P.IsFrobeniusAt σ ℓ → ((c σ : Rˣ) : R) = (ℓ : R))
subproblems.natural_proof:
1. Put Ω = AlgebraicClosure ℚ and G = Autℚ(Ω). For each n ≥ 0, the sibling finite_cyclotomic_character theorem applies to the positive integer p^n. Choose its character χ_n and its finite controlling field F_n. Let A_n(g) be the least nonnegative representative of χ_n(g), considered as an integer, and let a_n(g) be its image in 𝒪.
2. We first justify the primitive roots needed to compare levels, without requiring an additional conclusion from that sibling's interface. For every positive k, X^k−1 has k distinct roots in Ω, since it splits and its derivative does not vanish at a root. These roots form a cyclic group: for a finite subgroup of a field, form the least common multiple d of element orders; suitable powers give elements of each maximal prime-power order, whose product has order d because the orders are coprime. All subgroup elements are roots of X^d−1, so the polynomial root bound forces this element to generate the group. Thus a primitive k-th root exists.
3. Suppose n ≤ m and choose a primitive p^m-th root ζ. Then ξ = ζ^(p^(m−n)) has order p^n. The sibling action formulas give ξ^(A_m(g)) = g(ξ) = ξ^(A_n(g)): the first equality follows by applying g to the indicated power of ζ. Consequently p^n divides A_m(g)−A_n(g) in ℤ. Since p ∈ 𝔫, the image of p^n belongs to 𝔫^n, and ideal absorption gives a_m(g)−a_n(g) ∈ 𝔫^n.
4. The homomorphism laws for χ_n imply that A_n(1)−1 and A_n(gh)−A_n(g)A_n(h) are divisible by p^n. Their images therefore belong to 𝔫^n. Apply the sibling adic_character_lift theorem to obtain b : G → 𝒪ˣ satisfying b(g)−a_n(g) ∈ 𝔫^n for all n,g. This includes n = 0, where divisibility by one and membership in 𝔫^0 are automatic.
5. Write f = algebraMap 𝒪 R. Map b(g) and its inverse through f to obtain a unit c(g) of R. The ring-homomorphism laws and the homomorphism laws for b make c : G → Rˣ a homomorphism.
6. Locality gives f(𝔫) ⊆ 𝔪, since maximal ideals consist of nonunits and a local homomorphism sends nonunits to nonunits. Expressing ideal powers by finite sums of products yields f(𝔫^n) ⊆ 𝔪^n for every n.
7. If σ and τ agree on F_n, the finite-character conclusion gives χ_n(σ) = χ_n(τ), hence a_n(σ) = a_n(τ). Subtracting the two lift congruences shows b(σ)−b(τ) ∈ 𝔫^n. Apply f and step 6 to obtain c(σ)−c(τ) ∈ 𝔪^n. The field F_n is finite-dimensional, proving the required finite-field control.
8. Let ℓ ≠ p be prime, let P lie over ℓ, and let σ be arithmetic Frobenius at P. Since distinct primes are coprime, ℓ does not divide p^n for any n. The finite-character Frobenius conclusion says χ_n(σ) is the unit represented by ℓ modulo p^n. Thus p^n divides A_n(σ)−ℓ, and a_n(σ)−ℓ ∈ 𝔫^n.
9. Adding the lift congruence gives b(σ)−ℓ ∈ 𝔫^n for every n. Separatedness of 𝒪 makes b(σ) = ℓ as underlying scalars. Mapping through f gives c(σ) = ℓ in R, completing both conclusions.
proof_key_steps: Choose finite cyclotomic characters and controlling fields at every p-power level.
Establish primitive roots and derive compatibility of the chosen exponent representatives.
Verify the approximate homomorphism laws and apply adic_character_lift.
Map the resulting units into R.
Use locality to transfer congruences between maximal-ideal powers.
Use all Frobenius congruences and separatedness to obtain exact Frobenius values.

subproblems.title: A coherent inverse system of nonempty finite sets has a point
subproblems.statement: Let X_i be nonempty finite sets indexed by natural numbers. For each i ≤ j, let r_ij : X_j → X_i. Suppose r_ii is the identity and r_ik = r_ij ∘ r_jk whenever i ≤ j ≤ k. Then there exists a family x_i ∈ X_i with r_ij(x_j) = x_i for every i ≤ j. The transition maps need not be surjective.
subproblems.lean_statement: ∀ (X : ℕ → Type) [∀ i : ℕ, Finite (X i)] [∀ i : ℕ, Nonempty (X i)] (r : ∀ i j : ℕ, i ≤ j → X j → X i), (∀ (i : ℕ) (x : X i), r i i (Nat.le_refl i) x = x) → (∀ (i j k : ℕ) (hij : i ≤ j) (hjk : j ≤ k) (x : X k), r i k (Nat.le_trans hij hjk) x = r i j hij (r j k hjk x)) → ∃ x : ∀ i : ℕ, X i, ∀ (i j : ℕ) (hij : i ≤ j), r i j hij (x j) = x i
subproblems.natural_proof:
1. For j ≥ i, let A_ij be the image of r_ij in X_i. Each A_ij is nonempty. Coherence gives A_ik ⊆ A_ij whenever i ≤ j ≤ k.
2. For each fixed i, choose an index at which the cardinality of A_ij is minimal among j ≥ i. Every later image is contained in that image and has at least its minimal cardinality, so finiteness makes the images equal. Thus the intersection X_i∞ of all A_ij is nonempty and equals every sufficiently late image.
3. The adjacent map r_i,(i+1) sends X_(i+1)∞ into X_i∞: for any j ≥ i+1, coherence sends the image A_(i+1),j into A_ij, and membership for j = i is automatic. It is surjective on these stable subsets. Indeed, choose j beyond stabilization at both i and i+1. For x ∈ X_i∞ = A_ij choose z ∈ X_j with r_ij(z) = x. Then y = r_(i+1),j(z) belongs to X_(i+1)∞, and coherence gives r_i,(i+1)(y) = x.
4. Choose x_0 ∈ X_0∞ and recursively choose x_(i+1) ∈ X_(i+1)∞ mapping to x_i under the adjacent map. Step 3 supplies a lift at every stage.
5. For any i ≤ j, induction on j−i proves r_ij(x_j) = x_i. The base case is the identity transition. The induction step follows by factoring through j−1 and using the adjacent equality and coherence. Hence the chosen family satisfies every required compatibility.
proof_key_steps: Form the decreasing nonempty transition images at each level.
Use finiteness to obtain nonempty stable images.
Prove that adjacent maps between stable images are surjective.
Choose successive lifts and deduce all-pairs compatibility.

subproblems.title: Absolute arithmetic Frobenius approximation at a finite Galois level
subproblems.statement: Put Ω = AlgebraicClosure ℚ. Let E be an intermediate field of Ω/ℚ, finite-dimensional and Galois over ℚ. For every σ ∈ Autℚ(Ω) and every finite set B ⊆ ℕ, there exist a natural prime ℓ ∉ B, a valuation subring P of Ω with ℓ a nonunit, and τ ∈ Autℚ(Ω) such that τ preserves P, induces the ℓ-power map on its residue field, and satisfies τ(x) = σ(x) for every x ∈ E. Equivalently, P.LiesOverPrime ℓ and P.IsFrobeniusAt τ ℓ hold.
subproblems.lean_statement: ∀ (E : IntermediateField ℚ (AlgebraicClosure ℚ)) [FiniteDimensional ℚ E] [IsGalois ℚ E] (σ : (AlgebraicClosure ℚ ≃ₐ[ℚ] AlgebraicClosure ℚ)) (B : Finset ℕ), ∃ ℓ : ℕ, ℓ.Prime ∧ ℓ ∉ B ∧ ∃ P : ValuationSubring (AlgebraicClosure ℚ), P.LiesOverPrime ℓ ∧ ∃ τ : (AlgebraicClosure ℚ ≃ₐ[ℚ] AlgebraicClosure ℚ), P.IsFrobeniusAt τ ℓ ∧ ∀ x ∈ E, τ x = σ x
subproblems.natural_proof:
1. We first establish the finite arithmetic facts used in the argument. All finite fields of characteristic zero occurring below are number fields inside Ω. Their finite extensions are separable, since an irreducible characteristic-zero polynomial is relatively prime to its nonzero derivative. Extending an embedding across each algebraic generator by choosing a root of its transported minimal polynomial gives as many embeddings as the extension degree. Finite extensions are simple: for two generators α,β, distinct embeddings can agree on α+rβ for at most one rational r unless their β-images agree, in which case they never agree there. Avoid finitely many exceptional r; the resulting element has as many distinct images as the extension degree and therefore generates the extension. Induction treats a finite generating family. Scaling clears denominators to give an integral primitive element over ℚ. If K/F is finite Galois and H ≤ Gal(K/F), a primitive element α has |H| distinct H-translates. Its orbit polynomial has coefficients in K^H, while all these translates are roots of its minimal polynomial over K^H. The two degree inequalities prove [K:K^H] = |H|. For any intermediate field K′, normality and separability give [K:K′] automorphisms over K′, so their fixed field is K′ by this degree equality. Extending embeddings and restricting them then proves the fixed-field correspondence and the normal-subgroup quotient assertion.
2. Every finite multiplicative subgroup of a field is cyclic. Let d be the least common multiple of its element orders. Taking suitable powers supplies an element of each maximal prime-power order dividing d. Their product has order d: powers of two commuting factors of coprime orders can cancel only when both are one, because the intersection of their cyclic subgroups is trivial. Every group element is a root of X^d−1, so the polynomial root bound gives at most d elements, while the constructed element has d distinct powers. The root bound itself follows by division by X−a and induction on degree. In particular, for N > 0 the Nth roots of unity in Ω form a cyclic group of order N, since X^N−1 splits and has distinct roots. This argument also proves cyclicity of the multiplicative group of a finite field.
3. The integer ring O_K of a degree-d number field K is free of rank d over ℤ, Noetherian, integrally closed, and has fraction field K. Finitely many integral elements generate a finite module algebra, because their monic equations reduce powers. Conversely, if multiplication by x preserves a nonzero finite module in a field, choose module generators and a matrix of multiplication relations. The adjugate identity for xI minus that matrix makes its monic determinant annihilate the module, and hence vanish in the field. These arguments prove closure of integral elements under sums and products and transitivity of integrality. Scale a rational basis of K to integral elements. The trace pairing is nondegenerate: on a primitive-element power basis its matrix is the transpose of the conjugate-evaluation matrix times that matrix, whose Vandermonde determinant is nonzero. Evaluation at conjugates diagonalizes multiplication, so trace is the sum of conjugates. Traces of integral elements are rational integers; a reduced rational fraction satisfying a monic integer equation has denominator one. Therefore O_K lies between the lattice spanned by the scaled basis and its trace-dual lattice. A subgroup of ℤ^d is finite free: project to a coordinate, lift a generator of its cyclic image, split off this summand, and induct on the kernel. The lattice bounds give rank d. Ideals are such subgroups and their ℤ-generators also generate them as ideals, proving Noetherianity. Transitivity gives integral closedness; denominator clearing gives the fraction-field assertion.
4. Every nonzero prime 𝔮 of O_K is maximal with finite residue field, and (O_K)_𝔮 is a discrete valuation ring. For nonzero a ∈ 𝔮, its monic integral minimal polynomial has nonzero constant term, which belongs to 𝔮. Thus 𝔮 contains a rational prime ℓ. The quotient is a finite domain and hence a field. Its localization A is a one-dimensional Noetherian local integrally closed domain. Integral closedness localizes because multiplying a root of a monic equation over A by a common denominator outside 𝔮 makes it integral over O_K. To obtain a uniformizer, let 𝔞 be its nonzero maximal ideal and choose nonzero a ∈ 𝔞. The only prime containing (a) is 𝔞, so √(a) = 𝔞. The radical criterion follows by localizing at powers of an element outside the radical and contracting a maximal ideal. Finite generation of 𝔞 gives a least n ≥ 1 with 𝔞^n ⊆ (a). If n = 1, then 𝔞 = (a). Otherwise choose b ∈ 𝔞^(n−1) outside (a) and put x = b/a. Then x𝔞 ⊆ A but x ∉ A. If x𝔞 ⊆ 𝔞, the determinant argument of step 3 on the finite nonzero module 𝔞 makes x integral, a contradiction. Hence xy is a unit for some y ∈ 𝔞. For every z ∈ 𝔞, z/y = (xz)/(xy) ∈ A, so 𝔞 = (y). A nonzero element cannot belong to all (y^j): otherwise the ascending principal ideals generated by its quotients by y^j stabilize, and cancellation forces y to be a unit. Every nonzero element is therefore a largest power of y times a unit. Differences of these exponents define the discrete valuation on the fraction field.
5. Nonzero fractional ideals of O_K factor uniquely into prime ideals with integer exponents. For an integral ideal I, take the minimum local valuation of its finite generators at each prime. Only finitely many minima are positive: for nonzero a ∈ I, multiplication by a on an integral basis has nonzero integer determinant, so O_K/(a) is finite and has only finitely many primes. The prescribed product of prime powers has the same localization as I at every maximal ideal. Localizations detect membership and equality: if x ∉ J, a maximal ideal containing the proper ideal {r : rx ∈ J} detects this failure after localization. For inversion, I⁻¹ = {x ∈ K : xI ⊆ O_K} is finite, since multiplication by a nonzero element of I embeds it into O_K. Clearing denominators on finite generators shows that inversion commutes with localization. Thus II⁻¹ is locally, and therefore globally, the unit ideal. Denominator clearing extends factorization to fractional ideals, and local valuations give uniqueness.
6. For an integral ideal I define N(I) = |O_K/I|. Norms multiply and N((α)) = |N_(K/ℚ)(α)|; extend them multiplicatively to fractional ideals. To prove multiplicativity, distinct prime powers are comaximal: expand a sufficiently high power of a+b = 1 with a,b in the distinct primes. Chinese remaindering separates their quotients. At one prime, localization does not change the successive prime-power quotients, and a local uniformizer identifies each quotient with a one-dimensional residue-field space. Counting gives N(𝔮^e) = N(𝔮)^e. For principal ideals, integer row and column reductions identify lattice index with absolute determinant of multiplication by α; denominators handle nonintegral α. Only finitely many integral ideals have bounded norm: an ideal of norm n contains nO_K and corresponds to a subgroup of the finite additive group O_K/nO_K.
7. At most [K:ℚ] primes of K lie over a rational prime ℓ. Chinese remaindering gives a quotient of O_K/ℓO_K whose dimension is the sum of their positive residue degrees. Every nonzero prime of a number field F has a prime above it in a finite extension K. Indeed, localize the integral extension of integer rings away from the lower prime and take a maximal ideal upstairs. Its contraction is maximal: if a field is integral over a domain, a monic equation for the inverse of a nonzero element expresses that inverse in the domain, so the domain is a field. The local base ring has the specified unique maximal ideal.
8. In a finite Galois extension K/F with group J, J acts transitively on primes above a fixed lower prime. Otherwise Chinese remaindering supplies an integral a reducing to zero on one orbit and one on another. The product of all J-translates of a belongs to O_F, and has residues zero and one above the same lower prime, a contradiction.
9. The decomposition group J_𝔔 surjects onto the automorphism group of the residue extension. To identify the fixed elements of its image, suppose b̄ is fixed by that image. Choose integral a reducing to b̄ at 𝔔 and to zero at every other prime over the lower prime. The polynomial ∏_(h∈J)(T−h(a)) belongs to O_F[T] and reduces at 𝔔 to T^(|J|−|J_𝔔|)(T−b̄)^|J_𝔔|. Write |J_𝔔| = r^v u, with r the residue characteristic and r ∤ u. The coefficient of degree |J|−r^v is −u b̄^(r^v), so b̄^(r^v) belongs to the lower residue field. The r^v-power map is bijective on that finite field and injective upstairs, giving b̄ in the lower field. If the residue sizes are Q and Q^f, the Q-power automorphism has order f: its f-th power is the identity, and the polynomial root bound excludes a smaller positive power. There are at most f automorphisms because a generator of the upper multiplicative group generates the field and has minimal-polynomial degree f. Thus this automorphism group is cyclic of order f. A proper subgroup is generated by a d-th power of Frobenius for a divisor d > 1 of f; it fixes the Q^d roots of X^(Q^d)−X. These roots lie upstairs because this polynomial divides X^(Q^f)−X, and it has distinct roots. Its fixed field would therefore be strictly larger than the lower field, contradicting the fixed-element conclusion. Surjectivity follows.
10. For every finite extension K/F and nonzero lower prime 𝔮, [K:F] = Σ_(𝔔|𝔮) e_𝔔 f_𝔔. Localizing O_K over (O_F)_𝔮 gives a finite torsion-free module of rank [K:F] over a discrete valuation ring. It is free: project its fraction vector space to a nonzero coordinate; the finite image is a principal fractional ideal; lift a generator, split off that summand and induct on rank. Reduction modulo 𝔮, prime-power filtrations and Chinese remaindering give the degree formula. In the Galois case transitivity makes e,f constant, and orbit–stabilizer gives |J_𝔔| = ef. Step 9 then gives inertia order e. At an unramified prime there is a unique decomposition-group element inducing arithmetic residue Frobenius, of order f. Conjugation of primes conjugates this element, and restriction to Galois subextensions preserves it. Normalized local valuations also show that ramification indices multiply in towers.
11. Only finitely many rational primes ramify in a finite rational Galois extension K. Choose an integral primitive element. Its nonzero polynomial discriminant is an integer. Outside its prime divisors the distinct conjugates have distinct reductions, since their squared differences multiply to that discriminant. An inertia element preserves reduction, hence fixes the primitive element and is the identity. Step 10 gives unramifiedness. Every finite collection of number fields is contained in a finite rational Galois extension: adjoin all roots of the finitely many minimal polynomials of generators. Adjoining algebraic elements gives finiteness, embeddings permute these roots, and characteristic zero gives separability. Passing to such a container and using multiplicativity of ramification indices proves finiteness of ramification for general number-field extensions.
12. For a number field K, ζ_K(s) = Σ_(I≠0) N(I)^−s converges absolutely for Re(s) > 1 and equals its ideal Euler product. Step 7 bounds the prime-ideal sum by [K:ℚ] times Σ_ℓ ℓ^−Re(s), which is bounded by the convergent integer series. After removing finitely many factors, the inequality −log(1−x) ≤ 2x for 0 ≤ x ≤ 1/2 proves product convergence. Expanding finite products and using unique ideal factorization proves the series identity. Bounds using Re(s) are uniform on compact subsets of this half-plane. The next steps prove the pole and its ray-class refinement independently of prime distribution.
13. For a number field F put d = [F:ℚ] = r₁+2r₂ and W = ℝ^r₁ × ℂ^r₂. Factoring a primitive polynomial over ℝ and applying polynomial Chinese remaindering identifies F⊗ℚℝ with W. The complex splitting result used here is the fundamental theorem of algebra, specifically Complex.exists_root in the pinned Mathlib/Analysis/Complex/Polynomial/Basic.lean:35–53, also publicly identified by https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/db584cd6d46c92f209a44c0f1c829460d327499d/Mathlib/Analysis/Complex/Polynomial/Basic.lean#L35. An integral basis identifies O_F with a full lattice of covolume Δ_F > 0. A fractional ideal 𝔞 has covolume Δ_F N(𝔞), by the index and determinant formulas. Integrating the number of translates of a bounded measurable set over a lattice fundamental parallelepiped shows that volume larger than the covolume forces two distinct points to differ by a lattice vector. Apply this to half a symmetric convex body: volume larger than 2^d times the covolume forces a nonzero lattice point in the body.
14. The ordinary ideal class group is finite. Apply step 13 to an integral ideal 𝔞 and a product of intervals and disks of radii c N(𝔞)^(1/d), with c fixed sufficiently large. It supplies nonzero α ∈ 𝔞 with |N_(F/ℚ)(α)| ≤ c^d N(𝔞). The absolute norm is the product of the absolute real coordinates and squared complex moduli, by diagonalizing multiplication through the embeddings. The integral ideal (α)𝔞⁻¹ represents the inverse class and has bounded norm. Step 6 gives finitely many possibilities. Every fractional ideal class has an integral representative after clearing denominators, proving the assertion.
15. Unit logarithms form a full lattice. Give real places weight e_v = 1 and complex places weight e_v = 2, and put H₀ = {x : Σ e_v x_v = 0}. For a unit u, λ(u) = (log|u|_v) lies in H₀ because its absolute norm is one. Bounded logarithms bound all embeddings, and a lattice has finitely many points in a bounded set. Thus the logarithmic image Λ is discrete and its kernel is finite. That kernel consists exactly of roots of unity: roots have zero logarithms, and every element of a finite multiplicative group has finite order. For x ∈ H₀ use step 13 with radii c exp(x_v), whose weighted product is fixed. It supplies nonzero integral α with log|α|_v−x_v uniformly bounded above. Their weighted sum is log|N(α)| ≥ 0, which also bounds each difference below. Moreover |N(α)| is bounded, so only finitely many ideals (α) occur. Choose generators β_j for these ideals; α/β_j is a unit whose logarithm stays within a fixed distance of x. Hence Λ spans H₀. Choose a real basis from Λ and let Λ₀ be its integer span. A bounded fundamental parallelepiped contains representatives for Λ/Λ₀, and bounded sets contain only finitely many points of Λ. Thus this quotient is finite, say of order k, and kΛ ⊆ Λ₀. The subgroup argument for ℤ^r from step 3 gives a lattice basis for Λ. This also covers dimension zero.
16. Let a modulus 𝔣 consist of a nonzero integral ideal 𝔣₀ and specified real places. Its ray class group consists of fractional ideals supported away from 𝔣₀ modulo principal ideals generated by elements congruent to one at its finite primes and positive at its specified real places. It is finite. Forgetting these conditions maps it to the finite ordinary class group. The kernel is a quotient of elements having valuation zero at the modulus primes, modulo their residue and sign conditions. These residues and signs belong to the finite group (O_F/𝔣₀)ˣ × {±1}^𝔣∞. Denominators prime to the modulus exist by Chinese remaindering, and cross-multiplication proves independence of the resulting residue. The kernel is consequently finite. Every ray class has an integral representative prime to 𝔣₀: choose a denominator-clearing element congruent to one modulo 𝔣₀, and add a sufficiently large positive multiple of a positive rational integer lying in both the denominator ideal and 𝔣₀. This preserves denominator clearing and congruence and ensures all required positive signs.
17. Fix an integral representative 𝔞 of a ray class C, prime to 𝔣₀. Its nonzero integral ideals prime to 𝔣₀ are exactly α𝔞 with nonzero α ∈ 1+𝔣₀𝔞⁻¹ and the prescribed signs. At modulus primes this condition is the ray congruence because 𝔞 is locally the unit ideal. Elsewhere it is α ∈ 𝔞⁻¹, since 𝔣₀ is locally the unit ideal and 1 ∈ 𝔞⁻¹. Localization detects the global equivalence. Two parameters give the same ideal exactly when their quotient is a ray unit. The ray-unit group U_𝔣 has finite index in O_Fˣ by the finite residue-and-sign map. Its logarithmic image Λ_𝔣 is therefore a full lattice in H₀, with finite logarithmic kernel of some order w_𝔣 ≥ 1.
18. Choose a half-open fundamental parallelepiped B₁ for Λ_𝔣. For z ∈ W with nonzero coordinates put r = |N(z)|^(1/d) and b_v = log|z_v|−log r. Let ℛ consist of 0 < r ≤ 1, b ∈ B₁, the prescribed positive real signs, all choices of remaining real signs and all complex arguments. It is bounded and has positive volume: the radial, logarithmic and angular parameters give local coordinates with nonsingular derivatives in the interior. Its boundary is covered by finitely many Lipschitz images of bounded (d−1)-dimensional boxes and the origin. Indeed, the formulas ±r exp(b_v) and r exp(b_v+iθ_v) have bounded derivatives on closed parameter boxes, whose faces cover the boundary away from the origin. Each admissible ray-unit orbit has exactly w_𝔣 representatives whose logarithmic component is in B₁: there is a unique logarithmic lattice translate into B₁, and the logarithmic kernel acts freely on nonzero elements, preserving the sign conditions and r.
19. For any full lattice Λ, any translate z₀+Λ and t ≥ 1, the number of its points in tℛ is vol(ℛ)t^d/covol(Λ) + O(t^(d−1)). Tile W by bounded fundamental cells anchored at the translated lattice points. Cells whose closures avoid the boundary contribute equally to the point count and normalized volume. Subdivide the boundary parameter boxes into O(t^(d−1)) boxes of side at most 1/t. After dilation each image has bounded diameter and meets a uniformly bounded number of lattice cells, by the positive minimum separation of lattice points and the bounded cell diameter. Only O(t^(d−1)) cells can contribute error. The origin and half-open faces obey the same bound; when d = 1 it is O(1).
20. Apply step 19 to 1+𝔣₀𝔞⁻¹ and divide by w_𝔣. The norm bound N(α𝔞) ≤ X corresponds to t = (X/N(𝔞))^(1/d). Since covol(𝔣₀𝔞⁻¹) = Δ_F N(𝔣₀)/N(𝔞), the number A_C(X) of these ideals is κ_𝔣 X + O(X^(1−1/d)), where κ_𝔣 = vol(ℛ)/(w_𝔣 Δ_F N(𝔣₀)) > 0 is independent of C. Enlarging the error constant covers bounded X, t < 1 and exclusion of the zero parameter.
21. Summation by parts gives ζ_C(s) = s∫₁∞ A_C(t)t^(−s−1)dt for Re(s) > 1. The main term is κ_𝔣 s/(s−1). The error integral is holomorphic for Re(s) > 1−1/d: on compact subsets its differentiated integrands are bounded by integrable multiples of t^(−1−ε)(1+log t)^j. Uniform convergence of truncated integrals and their derivatives justifies differentiation. Thus ζ_C(s) = κ_𝔣/(s−1) plus a function holomorphic near one. For the trivial modulus, summing over the finitely many ideal classes proves that ζ_F has a positive simple-pole limit along real s decreasing to one. This derivation has used no Frobenius distribution or reciprocity.
22. Now let q be a rational prime and K = F(ζ_q), where ζ_q is primitive. This is a finite Galois extension, the splitting field of X^q−1. Its group J embeds in (ℤ/qℤ)ˣ by its exponent action, so is cyclic by step 2. Away from q the qth roots are units in the upper valuation ring, and reduction on them is injective. Unit membership follows from the valuation property and ζ^q = 1. If a nonidentity root ξ reduces to one, cancel ξ−1 in ξ^q−1 and reduce the resulting geometric sum; this would give q = 0 in the residue field. Hence inertia fixes ζ_q and is trivial away from q. Arithmetic Frobenius at a prime 𝔭 of F acts on ζ_q with exponent N(𝔭), because its residue action does so and reduction is injective.
23. Let T be any finite set of primes of F containing those above q. The free abelian group of fractional ideals supported outside T admits a homomorphism Φ_T to J, sending each prime to its Frobenius. Under J → (ℤ/qℤ)ˣ, its value is the positive rational ideal norm reduced modulo q; its numerator and denominator are prime to q. Set 𝔣₀ = qO_F times the product of the primes in T, and include all real places in the modulus. For α satisfying the ray conditions, the denominator ideal I = {x ∈ O_F : xα ∈ O_F} has no factor above q. Thus b = N(I) is prime to q, bO_F ⊆ I and bα is integral. At primes above q, α−1 ∈ qO_F locally, so bα−b belongs locally to qO_F. At all other primes q is a unit and bα−b is integral. Localization therefore gives bα−b ∈ qO_F globally.
24. On an integral basis, multiplication by bα is congruent modulo q to b times the identity. Taking determinants gives N_(F/ℚ)(bα) ≡ b^[F:ℚ] modulo q. Divide by the invertible denominator to obtain N_(F/ℚ)(α) ≡ 1 modulo q. This norm is positive because all its real factors are positive and the nonreal factors occur in conjugate pairs. Thus N((α)) also has residue one. Injectivity of J → (ℤ/qℤ)ˣ shows Φ_T((α)) = 1, so Φ_T descends to a homomorphism Art from the ray class group to J.
25. The homomorphism Art is surjective. Let H be its image and F′ = K^H. Since J is abelian, F′/F is Galois. Every prime outside T is unramified and has trivial Frobenius in F′, so splits into d′ = [F′:F] primes of residue degree one. Euler products give ζ_(F′), with factors above T removed, equal to the d′th power of ζ_F with factors in T removed. By step 21 both have positive simple-pole asymptotics, and the finitely many removed factors have positive nonzero limits. If d′ > 1, multiplication by (s−1)^d′ makes the first side tend to zero and the other to a positive number. Therefore d′ = 1 and H = J.
26. For a complex character ψ of J define L_T(s,ψ) = ∏_(𝔭∉T)(1−ψ(Frob_𝔭)N(𝔭)^−s)⁻¹ when Re(s) > 1. Character values have modulus one, so step 12 gives absolute and locally uniform convergence, including that of the Euler logarithm. A nontrivial ψ pulls back through Art to a nontrivial ray-class character θ. Its sum over the ray class group is zero: translation by a class where θ differs from one preserves the sum while multiplying it by a scalar different from one. The equal residues from step 21 therefore cancel in Σ_C θ(C)ζ_C(s). Ideal factorization and absolute convergence identify this series with L_T(s,ψ), because the modulus has support exactly T. Every nontrivial L_T(s,ψ) is consequently holomorphic near one.
27. Put m = |J|. At a prime outside T whose Frobenius has order f, the m characters take every fth root of unity exactly m/f times. Hence ∏_ψ(1−ψ(Frob_𝔭)X) = (1−X^f)^(m/f). Step 10 gives m/f upper primes, each of norm N(𝔭)^f. Multiplying these local identities proves that ζ_K with factors above T removed equals ∏_ψ L_T(s,ψ). Its trivial-character factor is ζ_F with its T-factors removed. The quotient by this factor has a positive nonzero limit at one, by step 21. All remaining factors have finite limits by step 26, so none can vanish at one. If m = 1 there are no nontrivial factors.
28. As real s decreases to one, Σ_(𝔭∉T) ψ(Frob_𝔭)N(𝔭)^−s = δ_(ψ,1) log(1/(s−1)) + O(1). Its difference from the Euler logarithm consists of terms of exponent at least two and is bounded by 2Σ_𝔭 N(𝔭)^−2. For the trivial character, the positive simple pole gives the stated logarithm. For a nontrivial character, divide L_T by its nonzero value at one and shrink a neighborhood until the quotient is within distance one of 1. The logarithm power series supplies a bounded logarithm there. On a connected real interval it differs from the Euler logarithm by a constant multiple of 2πi, since their exponentials agree and their difference is continuous. This proves the formula.
29. For each a ∈ J, character orthogonality gives Σ_(𝔭∉T,Frob_𝔭=a) N(𝔭)^−s = m⁻¹ log(1/(s−1)) + O(1). Indeed, m⁻¹Σ_ψ conjugate(ψ(a))ψ(b) is the indicator of a = b, by the finite geometric-sum identity in a cyclic group. Multiply step 28 by these coefficients and sum; absolute convergence justifies the rearrangement. Primes of rational residue degree at least two have norms at least ℓ², with at most [F:ℚ] primes above each ℓ. Their total contribution stays bounded as s decreases to one, as does any finite set's contribution. Removing them leaves a divergent sum. Thus infinitely many rational-residue-degree-one primes of F have any prescribed Frobenius a in F(ζ_q)/F, even after additional finite exclusions.
30. For every m ≥ 1 and finite set B₁ of rational primes, there is a prime q outside B₁ with m dividing q−1. For m > 1 define Φ_m by the primitive mth roots. The identities X^n−1 = ∏_(d|n) Φ_d(X), induction and division by monic integer polynomials prove Φ_m ∈ ℤ[X]; evaluating at zero gives Φ_m(0) = 1 for m > 1. Its degree is positive by step 2. Choose large positive t divisible by m and every prime in B₁ with |Φ_m(t)| > 1. A prime divisor q of Φ_m(t) divides neither t nor m and lies outside B₁, since Φ_m(t) is one modulo every prime divisor of t. In characteristic q, X^m−1 is squarefree. Its cyclotomic factors have disjoint roots. The residue of t, being a root of Φ_m, cannot have a proper-divisor order, for then it would also be a root of another cyclotomic factor. Its order is therefore m in (ℤ/qℤ)ˣ, proving m ∣ q−1. For m = 1, take a prime divisor of 1+k∏_(r∈B₁)r with k chosen so this integer exceeds one.
31. For a rational prime q and primitive ζ_q, C = ℚ(ζ_q) has degree q−1 and Galois group (ℤ/qℤ)ˣ, and q is totally ramified in every intermediate field. Indeed, Φ_q(X) = 1+X+⋯+X^(q−1), and Φ_q(X+1) is Eisenstein at q. To justify irreducibility, products of primitive integer polynomials are primitive by reduction modulo primes, so a monic rational factorization can be made monic integral. Modulo q both nonconstant factors of the shifted polynomial would be powers of X, forcing both constant terms divisible by q although their product is q. This contradiction proves irreducibility, and the q−1 conjugates give the asserted Galois group. The norm of 1−ζ_q is Φ_q(1) = q. For 1 ≤ i < q, (1−ζ_q^i)/(1−ζ_q) is integral by geometric summation and has norm one because numerator and denominator are conjugate. Its integral multiplication matrix has determinant one, so its adjugate gives an integral inverse. These quotients are units. Their product gives qO_C = (1−ζ_q)^(q−1) as ideals. The ideal (1−ζ_q) has norm q and is the unique prime above q, with residue degree one. Prime lifting and residue inclusion give a unique prime of residue degree one in each intermediate field. The degree formula then makes its ramification index equal to that intermediate field's degree over ℚ.
32. Return to the given E and σ. Normality makes g = σ|E an element of Gal(E/ℚ); let m be its order. By steps 11 and 30 choose a prime q > 2, unramified in E, with m ∣ q−1. Put C = ℚ(ζ_q). The intersection E∩C is unramified at q as a subfield of E and totally ramified at q as a subfield of C. Multiplicativity of ramification indices and step 31 force [E∩C:ℚ] = 1. Put M = EC. Since E is normal, M/C is Galois. Restriction embeds Gal(M/C) in Gal(E/ℚ), and the fixed field of its image in E is E∩C = ℚ. The fixed-field correspondence makes this image all of Gal(E/ℚ). Restriction is injective because E and C generate M, so [M:C] = [E:ℚ]. Restriction to the two factors is now an injective map between finite groups of equal size and identifies Gal(M/ℚ) with Gal(E/ℚ) × Gal(C/ℚ).
33. Choose a ∈ Gal(C/ℚ) of order m, possible by cyclicity and m ∣ q−1. Put h = (g,a), H = ⟨h⟩ and F = M^H. Then M/F is cyclic of degree m. Moreover M = F(ζ_q): the subgroup fixing both F and C is H∩Gal(M/C), which is trivial since projection from H to Gal(C/ℚ) is injective, both h and a having order m. Fixed-field correspondence gives FC = M.
34. Let T contain the primes of F above q, above rational primes in B, and above prime divisors of the nonzero discriminant of an integral primitive element of M. It is finite by step 7 and contains all primes ramified in M/F. Apply step 29 to M = F(ζ_q) and h. Obtain a rational-residue-degree-one prime 𝔭 outside T with relative Frobenius h, and choose an upper prime 𝔓 of M. Let ℓ be the rational prime below 𝔭. Then N(𝔭) = ℓ, so h preserves 𝔓 and acts on its residue field by the ℓ-power map. Rational inertia in M is trivial by the discriminant exclusion; hence h is also rational arithmetic Frobenius at 𝔓. Its restriction to E is g. At the contracted prime 𝔮₀ of E, rational Frobenius is therefore g and inertia is trivial. Also ℓ ∉ B.
35. Enumerate the nonzero rational polynomials f₀,f₁,…. Start with E₀ = E and obtain E_(i+1) by adjoining to E_i all roots of f_i in Ω. Each root set is finite by the polynomial root bound. Adjoining finitely many algebraic elements preserves finiteness. Embeddings preserve E_i and permute the full root set, so the stages remain normal over ℚ; characteristic zero gives separability. Every element of Ω is algebraic over ℚ and occurs among these roots. Thus the E_i are finite Galois fields with union Ω.
36. Recursively choose primes 𝔮_(i+1) above 𝔮_i, starting with step 34, using step 7. View V_i = (O_(E_i))_(𝔮_i) inside Ω and write 𝔞_i for its maximal ideal. These are nested valuation rings with contracting maximal ideals: denominators outside a lower prime remain outside an upper prime, and the prime itself contracts correctly. For j ≥ i, V_j∩E_i = V_i. If x ∈ E_i lies outside V_i, its inverse lies in 𝔞_i and remains a nonunit upstairs, preventing x from belonging to V_j. Their residue fields therefore embed compatibly, all in characteristic ℓ.
37. Let X_i be the finite set of rational automorphisms of E_i preserving 𝔮_i and inducing the ℓ-power map on its residue field. It is nonempty by residue-action surjectivity in step 9, applied over ℚ. Restriction defines coherent maps X_j → X_i for j ≥ i: lower fields are normal, primes contract, and residue embeddings preserve the power map. Identity and composition of restrictions give exactly the hypotheses of the sibling finite_inverse_limit theorem. Trivial inertia at level zero makes X₀ the singleton {g}.
38. Apply finite_inverse_limit to choose compatible g_i ∈ X_i. Their union defines a rational field homomorphism τ : Ω → Ω: any finitely many arguments lie in one stage, where all operations and rational scalars are respected. Their inverses are compatible because each restriction is the bijection g_i on E_i; their union is an inverse of τ. Hence τ ∈ Autℚ(Ω), and τ agrees with g, and therefore with σ, on E.
39. Put P = ⋃_i V_i. It is a subring because finitely many elements lie in a common stage. Any nonzero x ∈ Ω lies in a stage whose valuation ring contains x or x⁻¹, so P is a valuation subring. The union M₀ = ⋃_i 𝔞_i is a proper ideal by nesting and contraction. Its elements never gain inverses at later stages, while every element of P outside M₀ is already a unit at a stage containing it. Thus M₀ is precisely the set of nonunits of P. Since ℓ ∈ 𝔞₀, this proves P.LiesOverPrime ℓ.
40. Each g_i and its inverse preserves V_i, so τ and τ⁻¹ preserve P, placing τ in its decomposition subgroup. For x ∈ V_i, the defining residue action gives τ(x)−x^ℓ ∈ 𝔞_i ⊆ M₀. Every element of P occurs at a finite stage, and every residue class has a representative in P. Therefore τ induces the ℓ-power map on the residue field of P, exactly P.IsFrobeniusAt τ ℓ. Along with ℓ prime, ℓ ∉ B and agreement on E, this proves the stated conclusion.
proof_key_steps: Develop finite Galois theory and the integer-ring, valuation, ideal-factorization and residue-Frobenius facts.
Establish finite ramification and absolute convergence of ideal Euler products.
Use lattice geometry and unit logarithms to count ideals uniformly in ray classes.
Deduce equal positive residues of ray-class zeta functions without prime-distribution assumptions.
Construct and prove surjectivity of the cyclotomic ray-class Frobenius map.
Prove nonvanishing of the cyclic character factors and obtain prescribed degree-one prime supply.
Use a disjoint auxiliary cyclotomic extension and a diagonal cyclic subgroup to prescribe the exact finite Frobenius.
Build an exhausting tower of finite Galois fields with compatible primes.
Apply finite_inverse_limit to choose compatible finite Frobenius lifts.
Take unions of automorphisms and valuation rings and verify the exact absolute Frobenius predicates.

subproblems.title: Agreement on a field implies congruent representation actions
subproblems.statement: Let C be a commutative ring, M an additive commutative group with a C-module structure, J an ideal of C, G = Autℚ(AlgebraicClosure ℚ), U : G → End_C(M) a monoid homomorphism, and F an intermediate field of AlgebraicClosure ℚ over ℚ. Suppose U(δ)y−y ∈ J • ⊤ for every y whenever δ fixes F pointwise. If σ and τ agree on F, then (U(σ)−U(τ))y ∈ J • ⊤ for every y.
subproblems.lean_statement: ∀ {C M : Type} [CommRing C] [AddCommGroup M] [Module C M] (J : Ideal C) (U : (AlgebraicClosure ℚ ≃ₐ[ℚ] AlgebraicClosure ℚ) →* Module.End C M) (F : IntermediateField ℚ (AlgebraicClosure ℚ)), (∀ δ : AlgebraicClosure ℚ ≃ₐ[ℚ] AlgebraicClosure ℚ, (∀ x ∈ F, δ x = x) → ∀ y : M, U δ y - y ∈ J • (⊤ : Submodule C M)) → ∀ σ τ : AlgebraicClosure ℚ ≃ₐ[ℚ] AlgebraicClosure ℚ, (∀ x ∈ F, σ x = τ x) → ∀ y : M, (U σ - U τ) y ∈ J • (⊤ : Submodule C M)
subproblems.natural_proof:
1. Write N = J • (⊤ : Submodule C M). Every C-linear endomorphism v preserves N. Indeed, elements of N are finite sums of terms a • z with a ∈ J, and linearity maps such a sum to the corresponding sum of a • v(z), still in N.
2. Suppose σ and τ agree on F and put δ = τ⁻¹σ. Products of automorphisms apply the right factor first. For x ∈ F, δ(x) = τ⁻¹(σ(x)) = τ⁻¹(τ(x)) = x. Hence δ fixes F pointwise.
3. The hypothesis gives U(δ)y−y ∈ N for every y. Applying U(τ) and step 1 yields U(τ)(U(δ)y−y) ∈ N.
4. Endomorphism multiplication is composition. Since τδ = σ and U is a monoid homomorphism, linearity identifies this expression with U(σ)y−U(τ)y = (U(σ)−U(τ))y. This proves the conclusion for every y, without any finiteness or normality assumption on F.
proof_key_steps: Show that linear endomorphisms preserve ideal multiples.
Prove that τ⁻¹σ fixes F pointwise.
Apply the assumed stabilizer congruence.
Compose with U(τ) and use the homomorphism law.

subproblems.title: Trace respects ideal-valued congruence on a finite free module
subproblems.statement: Let C be a commutative ring, W an additive commutative group with a finite free C-module structure, J an ideal of C, and u,v ∈ End_C(W). If (u−v)w ∈ J • ⊤ for every w ∈ W, then tr_C(u)−tr_C(v) ∈ J.
subproblems.lean_statement: ∀ {C W : Type} [CommRing C] [AddCommGroup W] [Module C W] [Module.Free C W] [Module.Finite C W] (J : Ideal C) (u v : Module.End C W), (∀ w : W, (u - v) w ∈ J • (⊤ : Submodule C W)) → LinearMap.trace C W u - LinearMap.trace C W v ∈ J
subproblems.natural_proof:
1. If C is the zero ring, its only scalar is zero, which belongs to J, so the conclusion holds. Also every C-module is zero because w = 1 • w = 0 • w = 0. Otherwise choose a free basis of W. Its index set is finite: take finitely many module generators and the finite union of their basis supports. A basis vector indexed outside that union would have coordinate one where every linear combination of the generators has coordinate zero, contradicting nontriviality of C and generation. Thus write the basis as (e_i) indexed by a finite set, with coordinate maps λ_i : W → C.
2. Each coordinate map sends JW = J • ⊤ into J. An element of JW is a finite sum of a • w with a ∈ J, and linearity maps it to a sum of a λ_i(w), whose terms all belong to J.
3. For each basis vector e_j, the hypothesis and step 2 give λ_i((u−v)e_j) ∈ J for every i. These are the matrix entries of u−v. In particular the diagonal entries belong to J, so their finite sum belongs to J.
4. The trace equals the diagonal sum of the matrix in this basis, as in the pinned LinearMap.trace_eq_matrix_trace theorem. This identification is basis-independent: exchanging finite sums proves tr(XY) = tr(YX), which makes trace invariant under a change-of-basis conjugation. The diagonal entries of u−v are the differences of those of u and v, so their sum is exactly LinearMap.trace C W u − LinearMap.trace C W v. Step 3 therefore proves the required ideal membership.
proof_key_steps: Treat the zero ring and establish that a free basis has finite index set.
Show that coordinate maps send the ideal multiple JW into J.
Apply coordinates to the images of basis vectors under u−v.
Sum diagonal entries and identify the sum with the trace difference.

subproblems.title: Quadratic endomorphism expressions preserve ideal congruence
subproblems.statement: Let C be a commutative ring, M an additive commutative group with a C-module structure, J an ideal of C, a,b,d ∈ End_C(M), and s,r,u,v ∈ C. Suppose (a−b)y ∈ J • ⊤ for every y, s−r ∈ J and u−v ∈ J. Then ((a*a−s•a+u•d)−(b*b−r•b+v•d))y ∈ J • ⊤ for every y. Multiplication is composition of endomorphisms; no commutation hypothesis on a,b,d is imposed.
subproblems.lean_statement: ∀ {C M : Type} [CommRing C] [AddCommGroup M] [Module C M] (J : Ideal C) (a b d : Module.End C M) (s r u v : C), (∀ y : M, (a - b) y ∈ J • (⊤ : Submodule C M)) → s - r ∈ J → u - v ∈ J → ∀ y : M, ((a * a - s • a + u • d) - (b * b - r • b + v • d)) y ∈ J • (⊤ : Submodule C M)
subproblems.natural_proof:
1. Let N = J • (⊤ : Submodule C M). Every C-linear endomorphism preserves N, since it maps a finite sum of terms α • z with α ∈ J to the corresponding sum with the same scalar coefficients. Also α • z ∈ N whenever α ∈ J and z ∈ M.
2. Distributivity and the scalar rules give the ordered identity (a*a−s•a+u•d)−(b*b−r•b+v•d) = a*(a−b)+(a−b)*b−s•(a−b)−(s−r)•b+(u−v)•d. Expanding the first two terms cancels −a*b with +a*b; expanding the next two cancels +s•b with −s•b. No endomorphism factors are interchanged.
3. Fix y ∈ M. The first term evaluates to a((a−b)y), which lies in N by the image hypothesis and preservation of N. The second evaluates to (a−b)(b(y)), which lies in N by the same hypothesis applied to b(y). The third evaluates to −s • ((a−b)y), which lies in N by submodule closure under scalars and negation.
4. The fourth term evaluates to −(s−r) • b(y), and the fifth to (u−v) • d(y). They lie in N because their scalar coefficients belong to J, using ideal closure under negation for the fourth.
5. Closure under sums and the identity in step 2 show that the entire required difference evaluated at y belongs to N. Since y was arbitrary, this proves the conclusion.
proof_key_steps: Show that linear endomorphisms preserve ideal multiples.
Expand the quadratic difference without commuting factors.
Control the three terms involving a−b.
Control the two terms with scalar coefficients in J.
Combine the memberships by submodule closure.
